propositions.text: The appeal concerns the interpretation of PIPEDA regarding disclosure of a mortgage discharge statement.
propositions.quote: This appeal raises the issue of the proper interpretation of the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5 (“PIPEDA ”).

propositions.text: RBC is a judgment creditor seeking a sheriff's sale requiring a mortgage discharge statement from Scotiabank.
propositions.quote: The Royal Bank of Canada (“RBC”) is a judgment creditor of Phat Trang and Phuong Trang (the “Trangs”) and seeks a sheriff’s sale of the Trangs’ property, for which the sheriff requires a mortgage discharge statement.

propositions.text: RBC could not obtain the statement from the Trangs and moved to compel Scotiabank to produce it.
propositions.quote: RBC has been unable to obtain the statement from the Trangs and thus brought a motion to compel the Bank of Nova Scotia (“Scotiabank”), the Trangs’ mortgagee, to produce the mortgage discharge statement.

propositions.text: The Trangs and Scotiabank are not involved in the appeal; Privacy Commissioner appointed amicus curiae.
propositions.quote: The Trangs and Scotiabank are not involved in the present appeal, and counsel for the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (“Privacy Commissioner”) have been appointed amicus curiae.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns PIPEDA interpretation; RBC seeks a mortgage discharge statement from Scotiabank to enforce a judgment; Trangs and Scotiabank not involved; Privacy Commissioner is amicus.

propositions.text: PIPEDA governs personal information collection, use, and disclosure in commercial activities.
propositions.quote: PIPEDA governs the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by organizations in the course of commercial activities (s. 4(1)(a)).

propositions.text: PIPEDA generally prohibits disclosure of personal information without consent, with exceptions including debt collection, court orders, and legal requirements.
propositions.quote: In general, PIPEDA prohibits organizations from disclosing “personal information” without the knowledge and consent of the affected individual (see Sch. 1, cl. 4.3). There are a number of exceptions for which the requirement for knowledge and consent are not necessary for disclosure including where disclosure is “for the purpose of collecting a debt owed by the individual to the organization” (s. 7(3) (b)), “required to comply with . . . an order made by a court” (s. 7(3) (c)), or “required by law” (s. 7(3) (i)).

propositions.text: The issue is whether PIPEDA precludes Scotiabank from disclosing the mortgage discharge statement without the Trangs' consent.
propositions.quote: At issue is whether, in light of PIPEDA , Scotiabank is precluded from disclosing the mortgage discharge statement to RBC without the Trangs’ consent.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains PIPEDA's rules on personal information disclosure and the issue whether Scotiabank can disclose the mortgage discharge statement without consent.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and Scotiabank must produce the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and order Scotiabank to produce the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.

propositions.text: Two bases justify allowing the appeal: disclosure required by court order and implied consent by the Trangs.
propositions.quote: I find, as Hoy A.C.J.O. did, that there are two bases for allowing this appeal. First, disclosure is required to comply with an order made by a court. Second, the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure in the circumstances of this case.

propositions.text: Either basis alone suffices to dispose of the case, though both are present here.
propositions.quote: While it is not essential to have both of these bases to dispose of the appeal, both are present in this case, and each one of them, on its own, would suffice to dispose of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court allows the appeal, ordering disclosure based on court order and implied consent, either alone sufficient.

propositions.text: In April 2008, RBC loaned the Trangs about $35,000; they defaulted and RBC obtained judgment in December 2010.
propositions.quote: In April 2008, RBC loaned the Trangs approximately $35,000. The Trangs defaulted on the loan and on December 17, 2010, RBC obtained a judgment against the Trangs for $26,122.76 plus interest and costs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states RBC loaned the Trangs $35,000 in 2008; they defaulted and RBC obtained judgment in 2010.

propositions.text: The Trangs own Toronto property with a first mortgage held by Scotiabank initially for $262,500.
propositions.quote: The Trangs own property in Toronto. Scotiabank holds the first mortgage on the property, which was initially for $262,500.

propositions.text: RBC filed a writ of seizure and sale with the sheriff to sell the property under the Execution Act.
propositions.quote: In order to collect on its judgment, RBC filed a writ of seizure and sale with the sheriff in Toronto, which permits the sheriff to sell the Trangs’ property pursuant to the Execution Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.24, s. 9(1)

propositions.text: Execution Act s. 9(1) authorizes sheriff to seize and sell lands of execution debtor including trust lands and joint tenancy interests.
propositions.quote: 9. (1) The sheriff to whom a writ of execution against lands is delivered for execution may seize and sell thereunder the lands of the execution debtor, including any lands whereof any other person is seized or possessed in trust for the execution debtor and including any interest of the execution debtor in lands held in joint tenancy.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the Trangs' property has a first mortgage; RBC filed writ for sheriff sale under Execution Act s.9(1).

propositions.text: The sheriff refused to sell without a mortgage discharge statement from Scotiabank.
propositions.quote: The sheriff, however, refused to sell the property without first obtaining a mortgage discharge statement from Scotiabank.

propositions.text: Execution Act s. 28(3) states equity of redemption is saleable under execution subject to mortgage.
propositions.quote: Section 28(3) of the Execution Act provides that where land is subject to a mortgage, “[t]he equity of redemption in freehold land is saleable under an execution . . . subject to the mortgage”.

propositions.text: Execution Act s. 2(2) exempts principal residence from forced sale if equity does not exceed prescribed amount.
propositions.quote: In addition, s. 2(2) of the Execution Act states that “[t]he principal residence of a debtor is exempt from forced seizure or sale . . . if the value of the debtor’s equity . . . does not exceed the prescribed amount”.

propositions.text: The exemption amount ($10,000) was prescribed after the relevant time and does not apply here.
propositions.quote: Although s. 2(2) of the Execution Act has been in force since October 25, 2010, the exemption amount ($10,000) has only been prescribed since December 1, 2015 ... and therefore does not apply in the present case.

propositions.text: Mortgage discharge statement is necessary for sheriff to know Scotiabank's interest and rights between Scotiabank and RBC.
propositions.quote: The mortgage discharge statement is necessary for the sheriff to know Scotiabank’s interest in the property, and to ascertain the rights as between Scotiabank and RBC.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the sheriff refused sale without the mortgage discharge statement, which is needed to determine interests and rights under the Execution Act.

propositions.text: RBC served notices of examination on the Trangs who did not appear; RBC requested the statement from Scotiabank, which refused citing PIPEDA.
propositions.quote: RBC served the Trangs with notices of examination in aid of execution, scheduled for April 5, 2011. The Trangs did not appear. On November 15, 2011, RBC requested the mortgage discharge statement from Scotiabank. Scotiabank refused to provide the statement on the basis that PIPEDA precluded it from doing so without the Trangs’ consent.

propositions.text: RBC obtained a second examination order; Trangs again did not appear; RBC sought order compelling Scotiabank to produce the statement.
propositions.quote: RBC then obtained an order for a second examination in aid of execution, scheduled for February 17, 2012. The Trangs again did not appear. In May 2012, RBC sought an order compelling Scotiabank to produce the mortgage discharge statement.

paragraphs.summary: The Court recounts RBC's attempts to obtain the statement from the Trangs and Scotiabank, with refusals and motions to compel production.

propositions.text: The issue arises when a prior mortgage is in good standing but a subsequent creditor seeks to sell the property.
propositions.quote: The issue on appeal generally only arises when a prior mortgage is in good standing, but a subsequent mortgagee or judgment creditor seeks to sell the property.

propositions.text: If the prior mortgage is not in good standing, that mortgagee would enforce its own rights.
propositions.quote: Where the prior mortgage is not in good standing, that mortgagee would take its own enforcement proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes the issue arises when a prior mortgage is good, and a later creditor seeks sale; otherwise prior mortgagee enforces itself.

propositions.text: The motion judge denied RBC's motion based on binding Ontario Court of Appeal decision in Citi Cards v. Pleasance.
propositions.quote: The motion judge denied RBC’s motion on the basis that the Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision in Citi Cards Canada Inc. v. Pleasance, 2011 ONCA 3, 103 O.R. (3d) 241, was binding, and prevented him from ordering Scotiabank to produce the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.

paragraphs.summary: The motion judge denied RBC's motion relying on binding Ontario Court of Appeal precedent in Citi Cards.

propositions.text: In Citi Cards, mortgage discharge statements are personal information under PIPEDA and exceptions did not apply.
propositions.quote: The Ontario Court of Appeal held that a mortgage discharge statement was “personal information” for the purposes of PIPEDA and that none of the exceptions in s. 7(3) applied.

propositions.text: The court found s. 7(3)(c) exception circular if used as authority to order disclosure itself.
propositions.quote: Regarding the s. 7(3) (c) exception, where disclosure is required to comply with an order of the court, the Court of Appeal essentially concluded that it would be circular to find that s. 7(3) (c) was itself a source of authority to make an order for disclosure.

propositions.text: The s. 7(3)(i) exception applies only when the organization is required by law to disclose, which was not the case.
propositions.quote: The court further concluded that the s. 7(3) (i) exception, which applies when disclosure is “required by law”, only applies when the organization (here Scotiabank) is required by law to disclose information, which it concluded was not the case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court summarizes Citi Cards holding that mortgage discharge statements are personal information and exceptions to disclosure did not apply.

propositions.text: Following Citi Cards, the motion judge denied RBC's motion but questioned the result in obiter.
propositions.quote: Following Citi Cards, the motion judge denied RBC’s motion. In obiter, however, the judge questioned the result.

propositions.text: The judge noted mortgage discharge statements were commonly shared and questioned if Parliament intended to block judgment creditors from enforcing judgments.
propositions.quote: He observed that provision of mortgage discharge statements between banks in these circumstances was formerly commonplace, and he questioned whether Parliament intended to protect debtors by preventing judgment creditors from realizing on their court judgments.

paragraphs.summary: The motion judge denied RBC's motion but questioned whether Parliament intended to prevent judgment creditors from enforcing judgments.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal quashed the appeal as interlocutory and allowed RBC to examine a Scotiabank representative.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal quashed the appeal of the first motion on the ground that the motion judge’s order was interlocutory ... It was determined that RBC could seek to examine a Scotiabank representative.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal quashed the appeal as interlocutory and allowed RBC to examine a Scotiabank representative.

propositions.text: On second motion, the motion judge again dismissed RBC's motion, maintaining PIPEDA prohibits disclosure as per Citi Cards.
propositions.quote: On a second motion to compel Scotiabank to produce the mortgage statement ... the same motion judge again dismissed the motion. The motion judge indicated that he remained of the view that PIPEDA , as interpreted in Citi Cards, prohibited the release of the requested information.

paragraphs.summary: The motion judge dismissed RBC's second motion, holding PIPEDA prohibits disclosure as per Citi Cards.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority upheld the motion judge, finding mortgage discharge statement is personal information and no implied consent.
propositions.quote: The majority of the Court of Appeal upheld the motion judge’s decision on the second motion. It concluded that a mortgage discharge statement is “personal information” for the purposes of PIPEDA , and that the Trangs did not impliedly consent to disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement.

propositions.text: The majority declined to overrule Citi Cards and found exceptions under s. 7(3)(c) and (i) did not apply.
propositions.quote: It declined to overrule Citi Cards and observed that the exceptions for disclosure ordered by a court (under s. 7(3) (c)) and required by law (under s. 7(3) (i)) did not apply in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal majority upheld the motion judge, finding no implied consent and exceptions did not apply, declining to overrule Citi Cards.

propositions.text: The majority noted RBC could obtain the statement by prior consent in loan agreement or by motion under Rules of Civil Procedure.
propositions.quote: The majority observed that RBC could obtain the mortgage discharge statement in two ways. First, with foresight, RBC could have obtained the Trangs’ consent to disclosure by a term in its loan agreement. Second, RBC could apply for a motion under rule 60.18(6)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure ...

propositions.text: Such a motion would satisfy s. 7(3)(c) exception as it is based on separate authority, avoiding circular reasoning.
propositions.quote: Such an order would satisfy the exemption in s. 7(3) (c) of PIPEDA because it would be made on the basis of a separate authority, namely the Rules of Civil Procedure which would not cause the “circular” reasoning described in Citi Cards.

paragraphs.summary: The majority said RBC could get the statement by prior consent or a motion under the Rules, satisfying s.7(3)(c) exception without circularity.

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. dissented, would allow appeal on two grounds.
propositions.quote: Hoy A.C.J.O. would have allowed the appeal on two grounds.

propositions.text: First, an order need not be under rule 60.18(6) to be an 'order made by a court' under s. 7(3)(c).
propositions.quote: she would not require RBC to bring yet another motion to obtain disclosure of the statement. In her view, an order need not be sought under rule 60.18(6) to constitute “an order made by a court” within the meaning of s. 7(3) (c) of PIPEDA .

propositions.text: Second, a motion judge can exercise less caution for mortgagee examinations under rule 60.18(6)(a).
propositions.quote: Hoy A.C.J.O. held that where a party seeks an examination of a mortgagee under rule 60.18(6)(a) to obtain a discharge statement, a motion judge can exercise less caution than for examinations of other persons for other purposes.

propositions.text: She would overrule Citi Cards.
propositions.quote: She would have overruled Citi Cards.

paragraphs.summary: The dissenting judge would allow appeal, holding any court order suffices under s.7(3)(c), less caution needed for mortgagee exams, and would overrule Citi Cards.

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. found the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure as the statement is less sensitive information.
propositions.quote: Hoy A.C.J.O. concluded that the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure because the mortgage discharge statement is “less sensitive” information under cl. 4.3.6 of Sch. 1 to PIPEDA , and a mortgagor would reasonably expect that his or her mortgagee would be entitled to provide a mortgage discharge statement in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The dissenting judge found implied consent because the mortgage discharge statement is less sensitive information and disclosure is reasonably expected.

propositions.text: The issue is whether PIPEDA precludes Scotiabank from producing the mortgage discharge statement without express consent.
propositions.quote: The issue on appeal is whether PIPEDA precludes a mortgagee, Scotiabank, from producing a mortgage discharge statement to a judgment creditor, RBC, without the mortgagor’s express consent.

propositions.text: Specifically, whether the order sought is an 'order made by a court' under s. 7(3)(c) and whether the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure.
propositions.quote: More specifically, the issues are as follows: 1. Does the order sought by RBC constitute an “order made by a court” under s. 7(3) (c) of PIPEDA ? 2. Did the Trangs impliedly consent to disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement?

paragraphs.summary: The Court frames the issues: whether the order is a court order under s.7(3)(c) and whether the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure.

propositions.text: RBC argues Trangs impliedly consented as the statement is less sensitive and expectations depend on recipient and purpose.
propositions.quote: RBC argues that the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure since the mortgage discharge statement is “less sensitive” information, and the reasonable expectations of the Trangs cannot be properly assessed without considering who the recipient of the information is and the purpose for which they seek it.

propositions.text: RBC argues the order sought is an 'order made by a court' under s. 7(3)(c) due to court's inherent jurisdiction to order disclosure.
propositions.quote: RBC further argues that the order it seeks against Scotiabank is an “order made by a court” under s. 7(3) (c) of PIPEDA since the court’s inherent jurisdiction allows it to order disclosure of the statement.

propositions.text: RBC argues disclosure was 'required by law' under s. 7(3)(i) and permitted as Scotiabank was 'collecting a debt' under s. 7(3)(b).
propositions.quote: RBC also argues that disclosure was “required by law” under s. 7(3) (i) of PIPEDA , and that disclosure is permitted because Scotiabank was “collecting a debt” under s. 7(3) (b).

paragraphs.summary: RBC argues implied consent, that the order is a court order under s.7(3)(c), and that disclosure is required by law or permitted for debt collection.

propositions.text: Privacy Commissioner submits the order sought does not meet s. 7(3)(c) exception.
propositions.quote: The Privacy Commissioner submits that the order sought by RBC does not meet the exception in s. 7(3) (c) of PIPEDA .

propositions.text: While a motion under rules 60.18(6) and 34.10 can compel production, RBC did not reference rule 60.18(6)(a) in its motions.
propositions.quote: While a creditor may bring a motion under rules 60.18(6) and 34.10 against the mortgagee to compel production, in the present case, RBC made no reference to rule 60.18(6)(a) in its motions seeking production of the discharge statement.

paragraphs.summary: The Privacy Commissioner argues the order does not meet s.7(3)(c) exception and RBC did not rely on rule 60.18(6)(a) in motions.

propositions.text: The Trangs did not impliedly consent to disclosure of mortgage discharge statements containing sensitive personal financial information.
propositions.quote: The Privacy Commissioner further submits that the Trangs did not impliedly consent to disclosure. Mortgage discharge statements contain sensitive personal financial information.

propositions.text: Disclosure by mortgagee to judgment creditor is not within mortgagor’s reasonable expectations, assessed solely on mortgagor-mortgagee relationship.
propositions.quote: disclosure by the mortgagee to a judgment creditor is not within a mortgagor’s reasonable expectations, which are assessed based solely on the mortgagor-mortgagee relationship.

propositions.text: Disclosure was not “required by law” under s. 7(3)(i) of PIPEDA and not for purpose of “collecting a debt” under s. 7(3)(b).
propositions.quote: The Privacy Commissioner also contends that the disclosure was not “required by law” under s. 7(3) (i) of PIPEDA , and was not for the purpose of “collecting a debt” under s. 7(3) (b).

paragraphs.summary: The Privacy Commissioner argues the Trangs did not consent to disclosure, disclosure is not reasonably expected, and disclosure was not legally required or for debt collection.

propositions.text: PIPEDA is a federal statute governing personal information in commercial activities.
propositions.quote: PIPEDA is a federal statute that establishes rules governing the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by organizations in the course of commercial activities (s. 4(1)(a)).

propositions.text: PIPEDA is consumer protection legislation for the digital economy.
propositions.quote: In brief, it is “consumer protection legislation for the digital economy” (W. Charnetski, P. Flaherty and J. Robinson, The Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act : A Comprehensive Guide (2001), at p. 2).

propositions.text: Purpose of Part 1 of PIPEDA is to govern personal information respecting privacy and reasonable organizational needs.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this Part is to establish, in an era in which technology increasingly facilitates the circulation and exchange of information, rules to govern the collection, use and disclosure of personal information in a manner that recognizes the right of privacy of individuals with respect to their personal information and the need of organizations to collect, use or disclose personal information for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains PIPEDA governs personal information in commercial activities, protects consumers digitally, and balances privacy with organizational needs.

propositions.text: Part 1 of PIPEDA applies to personal information collected, used or disclosed in commercial activities.
propositions.quote: Part 1 of PIPEDA applies to personal information that an organization “collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities” (s. 4(1)(a)).

propositions.text: Section 5(1) requires organizations to comply with Schedule 1's 10 principles from the Canadian Standards Association Model Code.
propositions.quote: Section 5(1) states that “every organization shall comply with the obligations set out in Schedule 1”, which sets out 10 key principles derived from the Canadian Standards Association’s Model Code for the Protection of Personal Information (see Charnetski, Flaherty and Robinson, at pp. 5-6).

propositions.text: Clause 4.3 of Schedule 1 codifies consent as a key principle requiring knowledge and consent for collection, use, disclosure.
propositions.quote: Clause 4.3 of Sch. 1 codifies the third principle, consent. Under cl. 4.3.1, the general rule is that “[c]onsent is required for the collection of personal information and the subsequent use or disclosure of this information”, and cl. 4.3.2 states that “[t]he principle [of consent] requires ‘knowledge and consent’.”

propositions.text: Express consent is generally required but implied consent may be accepted in strictly defined circumstances.
propositions.quote: This third principle of informed consent is foundational to PIPEDA , and generally requires express consent. Yet, as I will explain, implied consent may be accepted in strictly defined circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court states PIPEDA applies to commercial personal information, requires compliance with 10 principles including consent, generally express but sometimes implied.

propositions.text: PIPEDA s.7(3) lists exceptions allowing disclosure without knowledge or consent.
propositions.quote: Section 7(3) of PIPEDA clearly provides a list of exceptions, for which knowledge and consent of the individual are not required for the disclosure of personal information: (3) For the purpose of clause 4.3 of Schedule 1, and despite the note that accompanies that clause, an organization may disclose personal information without the knowledge or consent of the individual only if the disclosure is . . . (b) for the purpose of collecting a debt owed by the individual to the organization; (c) required to comply with a subpoena or warrant issued or an order made by a court, person or body with jurisdiction to compel the production of information, or to comply with rules of court relating to the production of records; . . . (i) required by law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains PIPEDA s.7(3) allows disclosure without consent for debt collection, court orders, or legal requirements.

propositions.text: PIPEDA does not diminish courts' powers to make orders or interfere with rules of court or legally required disclosures.
propositions.quote: As a result of s. 7(3) , PIPEDA does not diminish the powers courts have to make orders, and does not interfere with rules of court relating to the production of records. In addition, PIPEDA does not interfere with disclosure that is for the purpose of collecting a debt owed by the individual to an organization, or disclosure that is required by law.

propositions.text: Section 7(3) intends to ensure legally required disclosures are not affected by PIPEDA.
propositions.quote: In other words, the intention behind s. 7(3) is to ensure that legally required disclosures are not affected by PIPEDA .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes PIPEDA s.7(3) preserves courts' order powers and legally required disclosures.

propositions.text: The order sought by RBC is an 'order made by a court' under s.7(3)(c).
propositions.quote: I find that the order sought by RBC constitutes an “order made by a court” under s. 7(3)(c), and I would order that Scotiabank disclose the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.

propositions.text: An order made by a court requires disclosure, unlike implied consent which only permits disclosure.
propositions.quote: An order made by a court requires disclosure, as recognized by the operation of s. 7(3)(c). This is in contrast, as we will see, with implied consent which results only in permission for a mortgagee to disclose the mortgage discharge statement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RBC's order is a court order under s.7(3)(c) requiring disclosure, unlike implied consent which permits disclosure.

propositions.text: RBC and Privacy Commissioner agree RBC can obtain an order meeting s.7(3)(c) exception.
propositions.quote: RBC and the Privacy Commissioner agree that it is possible for RBC to obtain an order for disclosure that meets the exception in s. 7(3)(c).

propositions.text: Disagreement is procedural: whether RBC had to invoke rule 60.18(6) specifically to obtain the order.
propositions.quote: The disagreement on this point is a procedural one, namely whether it was sufficient that RBC sought an order for disclosure by Scotiabank, or whether RBC had to have invoked rule 60.18(6) of the Rules of Civil Procedure specifically.

propositions.text: Relevant Rules of Civil Procedure provisions are rules 60.18(6) and 34.10(2).
propositions.quote: The relevant provisions of the Rules of Civil Procedure are as follows: 60.18 . . . . . . (6) Where any difficulty arises concerning the enforcement of an order, the court may, (a) make an order for the examination of any person who the court is satisfied may have knowledge of the matters set out in subrule (2); . . . 34.10 . . . (2) The person to be examined shall bring to the examination and produce for inspection, . . . (b) on any examination, including an examination for discovery, all documents and things in his or her possession, control or power that are not privileged and that the notice of examination or summons to witness requires the person to bring.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RBC and Privacy Commissioner agree on obtaining an order, but disagree on procedural rule invocation.

propositions.text: Motion judge and Court of Appeal majority found RBC's order is not an 'order made by a court' under s.7(3)(c) due to circularity.
propositions.quote: The motion judge and majority of the Court of Appeal concluded that the order sought by RBC does not constitute an “order made by a court” under s. 7(3)(c) on the basis that it would be circular to find that Scotiabank is required to disclose a mortgage discharge statement on the basis that disclosure is required by an order not yet made.

propositions.text: Citi Cards held it is circular to require disclosure based on an order not yet made.
propositions.quote: This follows from Citi Cards where Blair J.A. said: The “order” requiring compliance, upon which Citi Cards relies, is the order sought on this application. It is circular to argue that the Banks are required to disclose the mortgage statements because disclosure is required by an order not yet made.

paragraphs.summary: The motion judge and Court of Appeal majority found RBC's order is not a court order under s.7(3)(c) due to circularity, citing Citi Cards.

propositions.text: The court rejects the reasoning of the motion judge and Court of Appeal majority and would overrule Citi Cards.
propositions.quote: With respect, I reject this reasoning. I agree with Hoy A.C.J.O.’s reasoning at paras. 128-35 in support of her conclusion that Citi Cards should be overruled, and I would do so.

propositions.text: PIPEDA does not interfere with courts' ability to make orders.
propositions.quote: As I discussed above, PIPEDA does not interfere with the court’s ability to make orders.

propositions.text: Motion judge had power to order disclosure and would have done so if he thought he could.
propositions.quote: The motion judge had the power under either the Rules of Civil Procedure or the inherent jurisdiction of the court to order disclosure. Further, he would have ordered disclosure if he thought that he could, as Hoy A.C.J.O. recognized: “. . . had the motion judge thought he could order disclosure of the statement, it is clear from his reasons that he would have done so. It is also clear that it would have been appropriate to do so” (para. 112).

propositions.text: An order could and should have been made.
propositions.quote: I agree. An order could and should have been made.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects prior reasoning, agrees PIPEDA does not interfere with court orders, and finds an order could and should have been made.

propositions.text: Not pleading the rule number is not fatal to RBC's order request.
propositions.quote: In this case, the mere fact that the rule number was not pled is not fatal.

propositions.text: Requiring RBC to make another application specifying rule 60.18(6)(a) would be overly formalistic and harm access to justice.
propositions.quote: It would be overly formalistic and detrimental to access to justice to conclude that RBC must make yet another application, this time specifying rule 60.18(6)(a), to obtain the order it seeks.

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. found distinction between motions under rule 60.18(6)(a) and others for same purpose is artificial.
propositions.quote: Again, I agree with Hoy A.C.J.O.: “. . . any distinction between a motion brought under rule 60.18(6)(a) with the objective of obtaining a statement and any other motion brought, in accordance with the Rules of Civil Procedure, for the same purpose is artificial” since, in either case, the relief sought is substantively identical (para. 110; see also para. 96).

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. emphasized access to justice concerns and that RBC has made multiple motions and court trips.
propositions.quote: Critically, she correctly pointed out: It would fly in the face of increasing concerns about access to justice in Canada to dismiss this appeal and require RBC to bring yet another motion. A legal system which is unnecessarily complex and rule-focused is antithetical to access to justice. RBC has brought two motions and made two trips to this court over a several year period — simply to discern how much remains outstanding on the Trangs’ mortgage to enforce a valid judgment. [para. 113]

propositions.text: Not all litigants have RBC's resources; access to justice requires attention to all litigants' plight.
propositions.quote: I add that not all litigants have the resources RBC has available, or are able to make multiple trips to court. Ensuring access to justice requires paying attention to the plight of all litigants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds not pleading the rule number is not fatal, agrees with Hoy A.C.J.O. on access to justice, and rejects requiring another motion.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority held a party must show difficulty enforcing judgment and courts should be cautious about requiring strangers to appear.
propositions.quote: The majority of the Court of Appeal observed that a party seeking an order under rule 60.18(6) must demonstrate “difficulty” in enforcing its judgment, and that “courts should be reticent to require strangers to the litigation to appear on a motion” (para. 77).

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. concluded rule 60.18(6)(a) can be applied less cautiously for mortgagee examinations to obtain discharge statements.
propositions.quote: Hoy A.C.J.O. concluded, however, that rule 60.18(6)(a) can be applied less cautiously where a mortgagee is being examined in order to obtain a mortgage discharge statement. I agree.

propositions.text: Mortgagee is not a stranger to litigation as its interest in property is at issue and only mortgagee can produce discharge statement.
propositions.quote: As Hoy A.C.J.O. noted, a mortgagee is not a stranger to the litigation in the sense that its interest in the property is at issue as well — the sheriff requires the mortgage discharge statement in part to settle the priority between mortgagees and creditors. Moreover, in practice, only the mortgagee can produce a mortgage discharge statement.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Hoy A.C.J.O. that rule 60.18(6)(a) applies less cautiously to mortgagees, who are not strangers to litigation.

propositions.text: An order for disclosure can be made if debtor fails to respond to consent request or attend judgment debtor exam.
propositions.quote: I conclude that an order requiring disclosure can be made by a court in this context if either the debtor fails to respond to a written request that he or she sign a form consenting to the provision of the mortgage discharge statement to the creditor, or fails to attend a single judgment debtor examination.

propositions.text: A creditor with judgment, writ, and notice is entitled to an order for disclosure without cumbersome procedures.
propositions.quote: A creditor who has already obtained a judgment, filed a writ of seizure and sale, and completed one of the two above-mentioned steps has proven its claim and provided notice. Provided the judgment creditor serves the debtor with the motion to obtain disclosure, the creditor should be entitled to an order for disclosure. A judgment creditor in such a situation should not be required to undergo a cumbersome and costly procedure to realize its debt.

propositions.text: This is sufficient basis to order Scotiabank to produce the statement to RBC, and the court would so order.
propositions.quote: The foregoing is a sufficient basis to order Scotiabank to produce the statement to RBC, and I would so order.

propositions.text: There is more to the case beyond this basis.
propositions.quote: But there is more in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds an order for disclosure is appropriate if debtor fails consent or exam, and would order Scotiabank to produce the statement.

propositions.text: RBC argues the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement.
propositions.quote: RBC argues that the Trangs impliedly consented to the disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement by Scotiabank to RBC.

propositions.text: The court agrees with RBC that the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure.
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: RBC argues and the court agrees the Trangs impliedly consented to disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement.

propositions.text: Schedule 1, cl. 4.3.6 of PIPEDA allows implied consent for less sensitive information.
propositions.quote: Schedule 1, cl. 4.3.6 of PIPEDA acknowledges that consent for the purposes of the statute can be implied consent when the information is “less sensitive”: The way in which an organization seeks consent may vary, depending on the circumstances and the type of information collected. An organization should generally seek express consent when the information is likely to be considered sensitive. Implied consent would generally be appropriate when the information is less sensitive.

propositions.text: Consent can be given by authorized representatives such as legal guardians or power of attorney.
propositions.quote: Consent can also be given by an authorized representative (such as a legal guardian or a person having power of attorney).

propositions.text: Hoy A.C.J.O. correctly pointed out Citi Cards should have considered cl. 4.3.6 and might have been decided differently.
propositions.quote: In my view, Hoy A.C.J.O. correctly pointed out (at para. 117) that the court in Citi Cards should have considered cl. 4.3.6. Had it done so, as Hoy A.C.J.O. did and as I do here, Citi Cards may have been decided differently.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains PIPEDA allows implied consent for less sensitive info and agrees Citi Cards should have considered this clause.

propositions.text: Schedule 1, cl. 4.3.5 states reasonable expectations of individuals are relevant in obtaining consent.
propositions.quote: Schedule 1, cl. 4.3.5 of PIPEDA states that in obtaining consent, the reasonable expectations of the individuals are relevant: In obtaining consent, the reasonable expectations of the individual are also relevant.

propositions.text: Example: magazine subscription implies consent to contact for renewal; health info disclosure requires consent.
propositions.quote: For example, an individual buying a subscription to a magazine should reasonably expect that the organization, in addition to using the individual’s name and address for mailing and billing purposes, would also contact the person to solicit the renewal of the subscription. In this case, the organization can assume that the individual’s request constitutes consent for specific purposes. On the other hand, an individual would not reasonably expect that personal information given to a health-care professional would be given to a company selling health-care products, unless consent were obtained.

propositions.text: Consent shall not be obtained through deception.
propositions.quote: Consent shall not be obtained through deception.

paragraphs.summary: The court states PIPEDA requires consent to align with reasonable expectations and forbids consent obtained by deception.

propositions.text: Financial information is generally extremely sensitive, part of a person's biographical core.
propositions.quote: In terms of sensitivity, I agree with the Privacy Commissioner that financial information is generally extremely sensitive. As this Court observed in R. v. Cole, 2012 SCC 53, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 34, financial information is one of the types of private information that falls at the heart of a person’s “biographical core” (paras. 47-48).

propositions.text: Sensitivity of specific financial info is contextual, here assessed with public info and relationships.
propositions.quote: However, the degree of sensitivity of specific financial information is a contextual determination. The sensitivity of financial information, here the current balance of a mortgage, must be assessed in the context of the related financial information already in the public domain, the purpose served by making the related information public, and the nature of the relationship between the mortgagor, mortgagee, and directly affected third parties.

propositions.text: Motion judge and Hoy A.C.J.O. observed mortgage registration info is publicly available under Land Registration Reform Act.
propositions.quote: As the motion judge and Hoy A.C.J.O. observed, when mortgages are registered electronically on title, the principal amount of the mortgage, the rate of interest, the payment periods and the due date are made publicly available pursuant to the Land Registration Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.4, s. 3(1); R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 688, s. 2(2); and O. Reg. 19/99, s. 6.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds financial info is sensitive but context matters; mortgage details are publicly available by law.

propositions.text: Legislature balanced privacy and transparency in land registration, favoring transparency in public interest.
propositions.quote: The legislature decided to make this information available to the public, in part to allow creditors with a current or future interest in the land to make informed decisions. As the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario observed in Toronto (City) (Re), 2000 CanLII 21004: The land registration system requires that all pertinent information be made available as a matter of public record, and the extent to which this represents an invasion of any individual’s privacy, that result is justified and defensible. Transparency is integral to the public administration of the system, and has been incorporated into the statutory framework that regulates land registration in Ontario. Said another way, in implementing Ontario’s land registration system, the Legislature has considered and debated the appropriate balance between the right to privacy and the need for transparency, and has made a decision that transparency outweighs privacy, in the public interest. The rationale supporting the need to place personal information contained in land registration documents on the public record is based on the context of an individual land transaction. The public interest is addressed by ensuring that the parties to this particular transaction have all pertinent information involving the property. [p. 23]

paragraphs.summary: The legislature balanced privacy and transparency in land registration, favoring transparency for public interest.

propositions.text: Registration intent is to allow creditors to obtain information for guidance before becoming creditors.
propositions.quote: Making information about the mortgage public serves what Chancellor Boyd described as an intent of registration, albeit in the context of chattel mortgages: “The intent is, that persons who are about to become the creditors of others by parting with money or money’s worth, may, by searches in the public office, obtain information for their guidance . . .” (Barker v. Leeson (1882), 1 O.R. 114, at p. 117, quoted with approval in Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Co. v. Dearborn (1919), 58 S.C.R. 315, at p. 318).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites authority that registration aims to inform prospective creditors for guidance.

propositions.text: Public mortgage info is relevant to sensitivity of current balance, which is a snapshot in mortgage life.
propositions.quote: When creditors seek to enforce their legal rights against a mortgagor, the broad scope of the publicly available information about a mortgage is relevant to the sensitivity of the current balance of that mortgage. The current balance is a snapshot at a point in time in the life of a publicly disclosed mortgage.

propositions.text: Disclosing current balance furthers intent that parties have all pertinent property information and gives certainty to rough calculations.
propositions.quote: Disclosing the current balance of the mortgage furthers the intent of ensuring that the parties “have all pertinent information involving the property”. Disclosure gives certainty to the rough calculations that could already be made from the publicly available information.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds disclosing current mortgage balance furthers intent of full property info and clarifies rough public calculations.

propositions.text: Common law bank confidentiality exceptions include compulsion by law, public duty, bank's interest, and customer consent.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the common law recognizes that the implied obligation of a bank to not disclose information about those from whom it has obtained a security interest is subject to certain exceptions. In Tournier v. National Provincial and Union Bank of England, [1924] 1 K.B. 461 (C.A.), at p. 473, Bankes L.J. outlined four such exceptions: On principle I think that the qualifications can be classified under four heads: (a) Where disclosure is under compulsion by law; (b) where there is a duty to the public to disclose; (c) where the interests of the bank require disclosure; (d) where the disclosure is made by the express or implied consent of the customer.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites common law exceptions to bank confidentiality including legal compulsion and customer consent.

propositions.text: The state of account between mortgagor and mortgagee affects other creditors beyond their relationship.
propositions.quote: I agree with RBC that the state of account between the mortgagor and mortgagee affects more than just the relationship between them — it also affects other creditors.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the account state between mortgagor and mortgagee affects other creditors beyond their relationship.

propositions.text: The information at issue is less sensitive than other financial information.
propositions.quote: I find that the information at issue is less sensitive than other financial information.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the information at issue is less sensitive than other financial information.

propositions.text: Privacy Commissioner says only mortgagor-mortgagee relationship is relevant to reasonable expectations; Trangs-RBC relationship is irrelevant.
propositions.quote: The Privacy Commissioner submits that only the relationship between the Trangs as mortgagors and Scotiabank as mortgagee is relevant to assessing the Trangs’ reasonable expectations in the circumstances; the relationship between the Trangs and RBC has no role to play.

propositions.text: RBC argues the party receiving disclosure is relevant to determining the Trangs’ reasonable expectations.
propositions.quote: RBC argues that the party receiving the disclosure is a relevant consideration when determining the Trangs’ reasonable expectations.

paragraphs.summary: The Privacy Commissioner says only mortgagor-mortgagee relationship matters; RBC says recipient party matters for reasonable expectations.

propositions.text: Whole context is important to determine reasonable expectations of the individual.
propositions.quote: In my view, when determining the reasonable expectations of the individual, the whole context is important.

propositions.text: Office of Privacy Commissioner decisions support considering context in reasonable expectations.
propositions.quote: This is supported by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner’s consideration of context in various decisions: PIPEDA Report of Findings No. 2014-013, Re, 2014 CarswellNat 6605 (WL Can.); PIPEDA Case Summary No. 2009-003, Re, 2009 CarswellNat 6206 (WL Can.); PIPEDA Case Summary No. 311, Re, 2005 CarswellNat 6734 (WL Can.).

propositions.text: PIPEDA aims to promote both privacy and legitimate business concerns.
propositions.quote: the overall intent of PIPEDA is “to promote both privacy and legitimate business concerns”: L. M. Austin, “Reviewing PIPEDA: Control, Privacy and the Limits of Fair Information Practices” (2006), 44 Can. Bus. L.J. 21, at p. 38.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds whole context matters for reasonable expectations, supported by Privacy Commissioner decisions and PIPEDA's dual intent.

propositions.text: Mortgage discharge statement affects rights of others, not just private matter between mortgagee and mortgagor.
propositions.quote: a mortgage discharge statement “is not something that is merely a private matter between the mortgagee and mortgagor, but rather is something on which the rights of others depends, and accordingly is something they have a right to know” (2012 ONSC 3272, para. 29).

propositions.text: Legitimate business interests of other creditors are relevant to reasonable expectations of mortgagor.
propositions.quote: the legitimate business interests of other creditors are a relevant part of the context which informs the reasonable expectations of the mortgagor.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with earlier judge that mortgage discharge statement affects others' rights and business interests inform reasonable expectations.

propositions.text: Identity and purpose of party seeking disclosure are relevant context factors.
propositions.quote: Another part of the relevant context is the identity of the party seeking disclosure and the purpose for doing so.

propositions.text: Disclosure to someone exercising legal right differs from disclosure to someone curious or with nefarious intent.
propositions.quote: Disclosure to a person who requires the information to exercise an established legal right is clearly different from disclosure to a person who is merely curious or seeks the information for nefarious purposes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds identity and purpose of party seeking disclosure matter; legal right differs from curiosity or nefarious intent.

propositions.text: Reasonable mortgagor knows mortgage details are public and default can lead to sheriff seizure and sale.
propositions.quote: A reasonable mortgagor in their position would be aware that the financial details of their mortgage were publicly registered on title, and that default on the RBC debt could result in a judgment empowering the sheriff to seize and sell the mortgaged property.

propositions.text: Reasonable mortgagor knows mortgage balance will be provided to sheriff once writ filed.
propositions.quote: a reasonable mortgagor would know that the outstanding mortgage balance would ultimately be provided to the sheriff as a matter of law, once the writ of seizure and sale is filed.

propositions.text: Reasonable mortgagor knows property sale satisfies RBC debt subject to settling mortgage with Scotiabank.
propositions.quote: property would be sold to satisfy the RBC debt, subject to the settling of the mortgage with Scotiabank.

propositions.text: Reasonable mortgagor knows judgment creditor has legal right to obtain mortgage discharge statement by examination or motion.
propositions.quote: a judgment creditor in such circumstances has a legal right to obtain disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement through examination or by bringing a motion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a reasonable mortgagor knows mortgage details are public, sheriff gets balance after writ, sale satisfies RBC debt, and creditor can obtain discharge statement legally.

propositions.text: RBC seeks disclosure about asset it is entitled to realize on.
propositions.quote: RBC is seeking disclosure regarding the very asset it is entitled to, and intends to, realize on.

propositions.text: Reasonable borrower expects creditor can obtain info to realize legal rights if default occurs.
propositions.quote: a reasonable person expects that a creditor will be able to obtain the information necessary to realize on its legal rights.

propositions.text: It is unreasonable for borrower to expect creditor cannot recover debt by withholding info.
propositions.quote: it would be unreasonable for a borrower to expect that as long as he refused to comply with his obligation to provide information, his creditor would never be able to recover the debt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RBC seeks rightful asset info; reasonable borrower expects creditor can get info to realize rights; withholding info won't prevent debt recovery.

propositions.text: Reasonable person finds it appropriate for mortgagee to provide discharge statement to judgment creditor with writ filed with sheriff.
propositions.quote: a reasonable person would consider it appropriate for a mortgagee to provide a mortgage discharge statement to a judgment creditor who has obtained a writ of seizure and sale of the mortgaged asset from the court and filed it with the sheriff.

propositions.text: Judgment creditor with writ filed shows intent to exercise legal right needing disclosure.
propositions.quote: A judgment creditor who has completed these steps has demonstrated that it intends to exercise an established legal right that depends on the disclosure of the mortgage discharge statement.

propositions.text: RBC sought discharge statement via examination but writ filing alone suffices for consent to disclosure.
propositions.quote: RBC also sought the mortgage discharge statement through the examination process, but this additional step is not necessary.

propositions.text: Consent to disclosure for assisting sheriff executing writ was implicitly given when mortgage was given.
propositions.quote: Obtaining a writ of seizure and sale, and filing it with the sheriff, makes operational the consent to disclosure given by the Trangs concurrent with their giving a mortgage to Scotiabank.

propositions.text: Bank may not disclose discharge statement to any party without legal interest.
propositions.quote: this does not mean that a bank may disclose a mortgage discharge statement to any party who requests it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reasonable to provide discharge statement to judgment creditor with writ filed; consent was implicit at mortgage; bank cannot disclose to unrelated parties.

propositions.text: Trangs consented to disclosure; Scotiabank not precluded by PIPEDA from disclosing mortgage discharge statement to RBC.
propositions.quote: I find that the Trangs consented to disclosure. As a result, Scotiabank is not precluded by PIPEDA from disclosing the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Trangs consented to disclosure; Scotiabank may disclose mortgage discharge statement to RBC under PIPEDA.

propositions.text: Declines to decide if disclosure falls under PIPEDA exemptions for debt collection or required by law, as prior bases suffice.
propositions.quote: I decline to determine whether disclosure falls within the “for the purpose of collecting a debt” exemption in s. 7(3)(b) or within the “required by law” exemption in s. 7(3)(i).

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to decide if disclosure fits PIPEDA exemptions for debt collection or required by law, prior bases suffice.

propositions.text: Allows appeal and orders Scotiabank to produce mortgage discharge statement to RBC.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and order Scotiabank to produce the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and orders Scotiabank to produce the mortgage discharge statement to RBC.
